query: Starting from a eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies, what single intervention could overcome limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittleness while retaining or increasing strength? The hypothesis should address the tendency for dislocation pile-ups near internal boundaries to produce local stress concentrations, microcracking, and catastrophic damage during straining. Specify the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted strength and ductility relative to the untreated starting material, the applicable testing and operating conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A rapid thermal annealing treatment with a tailored heat treatment schedule will induce the formation of ductile nanoscale precipitates at the internal lamellar boundaries of the eutectic high-entropy alloy, thereby reducing dislocation pile-ups, minimizing local stress concentrations, and enhancing room-temperature tensile ductility while maintaining or slightly increasing the alloy's strength relative to the untreated state.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies that exhibits limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittleness, primarily due to dislocation pile-ups at internal boundaries.
generation.intervention: Rapid thermal annealing using a specifically tailored schedule (controlled high temperature for a short duration) designed to promote in situ interfacial nanoprecipitation.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile testing combined with microstructural characterization via in situ TEM/SEM to observe dislocation-interface interactions.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of ductile, nanoscale precipitates at phase boundaries within the lamellar colonies.
generation.mechanism: The induced nanoscale precipitates at internal boundaries provide extra slip-transfer pathways, which alleviate dislocation pile-ups that cause local stress concentrations. This leads to reduced microcracking and improved plastic flow during tensile deformation, enhancing ductility without sacrificing, and potentially increasing, strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: The treated alloy is predicted to exhibit increased tensile ductility (greater elongation to failure) and maintain or slightly improve its tensile strength compared to the untreated alloy, with microstructural evidence of reduced dislocation pile-ups and modified interfacial characteristics.
generation.baseline: The untreated eutectic high-entropy alloy displaying limited room-temperature ductility and dislocation accumulation at internal boundaries.
generation.boundary: The expected improvements are specific to rapid thermal annealing under controlled temperature and time durations; deviations in the heat treatment parameters or testing conditions (e.g., elevated temperatures) may not yield the same ductility-strength balance.
generation.uncertainty: While the microstructural modifications are expected to reduce dislocation pile-ups and improve ductility, the exact quantitative improvements in tensile properties are uncertain and require experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples from the same eutectic HEA batch with identical lamellar microstructures. Subject one set to the rapid thermal annealing treatment with the specified temperature and time parameters, while keeping the other set as untreated controls. Perform room-temperature tensile tests and in situ TEM/SEM characterization to assess dislocation dynamics.
measurements: Quantification of dislocation density and pile-up at interfacial boundaries
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the rapid thermal annealed samples do not show a significant reduction in dislocation pile-ups accompanied by improved tensile ductility (with maintained or enhanced strength) relative to the untreated samples, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The superior mechanical properties resulted from the obvious work-hardening behavior. The work-hardening behavior of the HEAs was systematically analyzed by adopting the modified Ludwik model. The Cr element improved the local deformation characteristics, and the coordinated deformation of the dual phase was carried out, improving the nonuniform strain and promoting the strength and ductility balance of the alloys.

The eutectic AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy, with an fcc/B2 dual-phase constitution and a uniform and fine lamellar microstructure, exhibited the combination of both high fracture strength and high ductility, which has never been achieved in previously reported HEAs. The room temperature tensile test showed a fracture stress of 944 MPa and an elongation of 25.6%, from the engineering stress-strain curve given in Fig. 4a. These values converted to 1186 MPa and 22.8% in the true stress/strain condition. Noteworthily, this alloy exhibited an ultra-high strain hardening behavior, having the proof stress (the proof stress is determined by shifting the linear elastic curve to 0.2% strain. We choose to not to call it the yield stress, as the mechanism for such a low elastic limit is still unclear at this stage.) of 75 MPa but reaching the fracture stress close to 1.2 GPa. At elevated temperatures of 600 and 700°C (Fig. 4b), the proof stress, fracture stress and elongation were 95 MPa, 806 MPa, 33.7%, and 108 MPa, 538 MPa, 22.9%, respectively, both in the true stress/strain condition. We believe that the excellent strength, ductility and toughness of this high-entropy alloy results directly from this synergy of intrinsic (plasticity related) and extrinsic (shielding related) mechanisms, which (unlike traditional toughening mechanisms involving mainly precipitates and/or boundaries) primarily result from its special material characteristics of a low average SFE with possible variation of local SFE (that modulates the behaviour of full and partial dislocations locally), and high lattice friction (that provides strengthening from the increased resistance to the planar slip of dislocations and its influence on the motion of partial dislocations), the low SFE further contributing to the remarkable formation of nanoscale crack bridges within a few hundred nanometres of the crack tip. (Further deliberations on the controlling factors for this synergy of deformation mechanisms are described in Supplementary Note 3). chosen.technique: rapid thermal annealing to induce interfacial precipitation
chosen.conditions: Room-temperature tensile tests complemented by in situ TEM to observe dislocation dynamics at modified internal boundaries
chosen.why: This intervention most directly addresses the identified unexplained behavior—the dislocation pile‐ups at internal boundaries—by modifying the microstructural interface via a controlled heat treatment. The brief high-temperature exposure promotes the formation of ductile nanoprecipitates or interfacial phases that can absorb or transmit dislocations, thus mitigating local stress concentrations. This approach is common in materials science for high-entropy alloys, is experimentally feasible, and is expected to improve ductility while maintaining or even increasing strength relative to the untreated eutectic alloy.
